Wave Properties.intro: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Understanding the properties and types of waves is essential for all of P6.
Wave Properties.mnemonic: "Tall Waves Frequently Travel Long" — Transverse, Wavelength, Frequency, Time period, Longitudinal. For the wave equation v = fλ: 'Very Fast Lamborghinis' (v = f × λ).

sections.title: Types of Wave
sections.text: Waves are disturbances that transfer energy from one place to another. There are two main types depending on the direction of oscillation relative to energy transfer.
points: Transverse waves — oscillation perpendicular to direction of travel; e.g. light, water, seismic S-waves
Longitudinal waves — oscillation parallel to direction of travel; e.g. sound, seismic P-waves; have compressions and rarefactions
Compressions — regions of high pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed together
Rarefactions — regions of low pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles spread apart
Energy transfer — waves transfer energy but the medium itself does not move with the wave

sections.title: Wave Properties
sections.text: Every wave can be described by a set of measurable properties. These properties are related by the wave equation.
points: Amplitude (A) — maximum displacement from equilibrium (m); larger amplitude = more energy carried
Wavelength (λ) — distance from one point to the next identical point, e.g. crest to crest (m)
Frequency (f) — number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
Time period (T) — time for one complete wave to pass a point: T = 1/f (s); e.g. f = 50 Hz → T = 0.02 s
Wave speed (v) — speed at which the wave pattern travels through the medium (m/s)

sections.title: Wave Equation
sections.text: The wave equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength. It applies to all waves — sound, light and all EM waves.
points: v = f × λ — wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
Worked example — a wave has f = 200 Hz and λ = 1.7 m: v = 200 × 1.7 = 340 m/s (speed of sound in air)
Rearranging for frequency — f = v ÷ λ; e.g. v = 3×10⁸ m/s, λ = 0.01 m → f = 3×10¹⁰ Hz
Rearranging for wavelength — λ = v ÷ f; e.g. radio station at 100 MHz: λ = 3×10⁸ ÷ 10⁸ = 3 m
T = 1/f — period and frequency are reciprocals; e.g. f = 440 Hz (musical A) → T = 0.00227 s
All EM waves in vacuum — speed = 3 × 10⁸ m/s regardless of frequency or wavelength

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: v = f × λ (Wave speed = frequency × wavelength). Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m.

keyTerms.def: Maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position; determines energy/loudness/brightness
Distance between two adjacent points in phase on a wave, e.g. crest to crest (symbol λ, unit: m)
Number of complete wave cycles per second — measured in hertz (Hz)
Time taken for one complete wave cycle to pass a point; T = 1/f (unit: seconds)
Wave where oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, water waves)
Wave where oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound waves)
The speed at which the wave pattern moves through a medium, related by v = fλ
Region of high pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are close together

examTips: v = fλ — the most important wave equation. Rearrange to find f or λ. Always check units: speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m.
T = 1/f — period and frequency are inversely related. If f = 50 Hz then T = 0.02 s. Show this working in calculation questions.
Amplitude affects intensity/loudness/brightness; frequency affects pitch (sound) or colour (light) — AQA often asks you to state which property is changed.
In transverse waves, oscillation is at 90° to the direction of travel. In longitudinal waves, oscillation is along the direction of travel — use these exact phrases in AQA 6-mark questions.
commonMistakes: Confusing transverse (perpendicular) and longitudinal (parallel) waves — remember: Trans = across, Long = along.
Confusing amplitude (maximum displacement from equilibrium) with wavelength (distance between peaks) — amplitude is height of wave, wavelength is length along it.
Writing the wave equation as v = f/λ or v = λ/f — it is always v = f × λ (multiplication, not division).
Assuming wave speed changes when frequency changes — in the same medium, wave speed is constant; only wavelength changes.
clozePassages: Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — examples include light and water waves. Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer — sound waves are longitudinal. All waves have amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and wave speed. The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is speed, f is frequency, and λ is wavelength.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement from the rest position. A larger amplitude means more energy is being transferred. The wavelength is the distance between successive crests or compressions. The frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Period is the time for one complete wave. Frequency and period are related by: f = 1/T.

The wave equation v = fλ relates wave speed, frequency, and wavelength. If frequency increases and speed remains constant, wavelength decreases. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). Sound travels much more slowly — about 340 m/s in air. Waves can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, and can show interference. These behaviours are explained by the wave model.

Reflection and Refraction.intro: Waves change direction when they reflect off surfaces or refract as they change speed at a boundary. These phenomena are key to how lenses, mirrors and optical fibres work.
Reflection and Refraction.mnemonic: "Normal Incidence Reflects, Changes Direction" — Angles from Normal, Incidence = Reflection, Refraction Changes Direction. For TIR: 'Denser to Less dense, Critical angle, Total reflection' = DLC-T.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.text: When a wave hits a surface it bounces back. The law of reflection governs exactly how it bounces.
points: Law of reflection — angle of incidence = angle of reflection; both measured from the normal
Normal — imaginary line perpendicular to surface at point of incidence; all angles measured from this
Specular reflection — smooth surface (e.g. mirror); parallel rays stay parallel after reflection
Diffuse reflection — rough surface; parallel rays scatter in all directions — allows us to see non-shiny objects
Plane mirror image — virtual (cannot be projected), upright, laterally inverted, same size as object, same distance behind mirror as object is in front

sections.title: Refraction
sections.text: Refraction occurs when waves cross a boundary between two media and change speed, causing a change in direction.
points: Cause of refraction — waves change speed at a boundary between media; change in speed → change in direction
Towards normal — light entering denser medium (e.g. air → glass) slows down and bends towards normal
Away from normal — light entering less dense medium (e.g. glass → air) speeds up and bends away from normal
Frequency unchanged — refraction changes speed and wavelength but NOT frequency
No bend if normal incidence — if light hits boundary at exactly 90° (along normal) it slows but does not change direction

sections.title: Total Internal Reflection
sections.text: When light in a denser medium hits the boundary at a large enough angle, it reflects completely instead of refracting — this is total internal reflection (TIR).
points: Critical angle — the angle of incidence above which TIR occurs; for glass ≈ 42°
Conditions for TIR — must travel from denser to less dense medium AND angle of incidence must exceed critical angle
Optical fibres — use TIR to carry light signals; used in telecommunications (faster than electrical signals) and medicine
Endoscopes — bundles of optical fibres used by doctors to see inside the body without surgery
Periscopes and binoculars — use glass prisms to achieve TIR and redirect light through 90° or 180°

keyTerms.def: A line perpendicular to a surface at the point where a ray hits; all angles in optics are measured from the normal
Angle between the incoming ray and the normal at the point of incidence
Angle between the reflected ray and the normal; always equal to the angle of incidence
Change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary due to a change in speed
Complete reflection at a boundary when light in a denser medium exceeds the critical angle
The minimum angle of incidence (measured from normal) at which total internal reflection occurs
Reflection from a smooth surface where parallel rays remain parallel after bouncing
Thin glass or plastic fibre that carries light signals by repeated total internal reflection

examTips: All angles measured from the NORMAL, not the surface — a very common error that loses marks. Draw the normal first before drawing rays in diagrams.
Refraction: towards normal = slower (denser medium). Away from normal = faster (less dense medium). Use this as a memory check when drawing refraction diagrams.
Total internal reflection requires TWO conditions: (1) denser to less dense medium AND (2) angle of incidence > critical angle. Stating only one condition loses a mark.

AQA may ask you to explain why optical fibres use TIR. State: light hits the inner boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected and travels along the fibre.
commonMistakes: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal — always draw the normal as a dashed line perpendicular to the surface and measure from that.
Saying refraction changes frequency — it changes speed and wavelength but NOT frequency. Frequency is determined by the source.
Forgetting that TIR can only happen when going from a denser medium to a less dense medium (e.g. glass to air), not the other way round.
Drawing refraction diagrams with the ray bending the wrong way — check: slower medium = bends towards normal; faster medium = bends away.
clozePassages: Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface). Smooth surfaces produce regular (specular) reflection; rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection. Mirrors use regular reflection. The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright, laterally inverted, and the same size as the object.

Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another with a different speed. When light passes from air to glass, it slows down and bends towards the normal. When passing from glass to air, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The greater the change in speed, the greater the angle of refraction. Refraction explains why objects appear displaced when viewed through water or glass.

Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle. The light is completely reflected back into the denser medium. This principle is used in optical fibres — light travels along the fibre by repeated total internal reflection. Optical fibres are used in telecommunications to transmit data at high speed over long distances, and in medicine for endoscopes.

Sound.intro: Sound is a longitudinal wave that requires a medium to travel through. Understanding its properties and how it is heard is required for P6.
Sound.mnemonic: "Loud Parrots Can't Understand Silence" — Longitudinal, Pressure waves, Compressions, Ultrasound (>20kHz), Speed ~340 m/s in air. For sonar: 'Half the time, full the distance' (d = v × t/2).

sections.title: Nature of Sound
sections.text: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave that travels as pressure variations through a medium. It cannot exist without particles to vibrate.
points: Longitudinal wave — particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel; creates compressions and rarefactions
Requires a medium — sound cannot travel through a vacuum (no particles to vibrate); proven by bell-in-jar experiment
Speed in air — approximately 340 m/s; increases in liquids (≈1500 m/s in water) and solids (≈5000 m/s in steel)
Pitch — determined by frequency; higher frequency = higher pitch
Loudness — determined by amplitude; greater amplitude = louder sound = more energy transferred

sections.title: Hearing Range and Ultrasound
sections.text: Humans can hear a limited range of frequencies. Sound beyond this range still obeys the same wave rules and has important practical uses.
points: Human hearing range — 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); varies with age (upper limit decreases with age)
Ultrasound — frequency above 20,000 Hz; too high for humans to hear; used in medicine and industry
Medical scanning — ultrasound pulses reflect off tissue boundaries; timing of reflections builds up an image (safer than X-rays, no ionising radiation)
Industrial uses — detecting cracks in materials, cleaning delicate instruments
Infrasound — below 20 Hz; used by elephants and whales for long-distance communication; generated by earthquakes

sections.title: Echoes and Sonar
sections.text: Reflected sound creates echoes. This principle is exploited in sonar systems to measure distances underwater.
points: Echo — reflection of a sound wave from a surface; heard as a delayed copy of original sound
Sonar formula — distance = (wave speed × time) ÷ 2; the ÷2 accounts for sound travelling to object and back: d = v × t/2
Worked example — echo returns after 0.4 s, v = 1500 m/s in water: d = 1500 × 0.4 / 2 = 300 m depth
Applications — mapping sea floor, locating submarines, fish finders, measuring distance to objects
Oscilloscope — used to display sound waves; amplitude shown by height, frequency by how many waves fit in a given time

keyTerms.def: Longitudinal pressure wave — requires a medium to travel; cannot pass through a vacuum
Region of high pressure in a sound wave where air particles are pushed closer together
Region of low pressure in a sound wave where air particles spread apart
Sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz — above human hearing range; used in medical imaging and sonar
Sound with frequency below 20 Hz — below human hearing range; used by some large animals
Reflection of a sound wave from a surface, heard as a delayed repetition of the original sound
Perceived highness or lowness of a sound — determined by frequency
System using reflected ultrasound pulses to measure distances underwater; d = v × t/2

examTips: Sound is longitudinal; light is transverse — AQA frequently asks you to state the type of wave and explain what this means in terms of particle oscillation direction.
Speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s. Sound travels faster in denser materials (liquids > gases; solids > liquids) because particles are closer together and transmit vibrations more quickly.
Ultrasound: f > 20,000 Hz. Infrasound: f < 20 Hz. Use the sonar equation d = v × t/2 and remember to halve the time because the pulse makes a return journey.
When comparing sound on an oscilloscope: louder = taller waves (greater amplitude); higher pitch = more waves in same space (higher frequency). AQA often gives oscilloscope diagrams to interpret.
commonMistakes: Saying sound travels faster in less dense materials — it is the opposite. Sound travels fastest in solids because particles are closest together and can transmit vibrations quickly.
Confusing pitch (frequency) with loudness (amplitude) — higher frequency = higher pitch; greater amplitude = louder.
Forgetting to divide by 2 in sonar/echo calculations — sound travels to the object AND back, so the total distance is twice the one-way distance.
Saying sound can travel through a vacuum — it cannot. Space is (nearly) silent because there are no particles to carry the vibration.
clozePassages: Sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrating objects. It travels as alternating regions of high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions) through a medium. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate. The speed of sound is approximately 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and fastest in solids. Sound waves can be reflected as echoes and refracted at boundaries between media.

The frequency of a sound wave determines its pitch. High frequency sounds have high pitch. The typical range of human hearing is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound; sounds above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound. Ultrasound is used in medical imaging, sonar, and measuring distances. The amplitude of a sound wave determines its loudness — a larger amplitude means a louder sound and more energy.

Ultrasound has frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing (20,000 Hz). It is used in medicine for prenatal scanning — ultrasound pulses are sent into the body and reflected at boundaries between tissues. The reflected pulses are detected and used to build up an image. Ultrasound is safer than X-rays for imaging soft tissue. It is also used in sonar to map the sea floor, and in industrial applications to detect cracks in materials.

Electromagnetic Spectrum.intro: The electromagnetic spectrum is a family of transverse waves that all travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength.
Electromagnetic Spectrum.mnemonic: "Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns" — Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma. Going from Radio to Gamma: frequency increases, wavelength decreases, energy increases, more ionising.

sections.title: The EM Spectrum
sections.text: The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of transverse waves. All types share common properties but differ in frequency and wavelength.
points: Common properties — all EM waves: travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; are transverse; can travel through a vacuum; transfer energy
Order (low to high frequency) — Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma
Visible light range — wavelengths from ~700 nm (red) to ~400 nm (violet); ROY G BIV (Red Orange Yellow Green Blue Indigo Violet)
Energy and frequency — higher frequency = more energy per photon = more ionising radiation
Wave equation applies — v = fλ applies to all EM waves; e.g. radio at 100 MHz: λ = 3×10⁸ / 10⁸ = 3 m

sections.title: Uses of EM Waves
sections.text: Each part of the EM spectrum has specific uses based on its properties — particularly its ability to penetrate materials and carry information.
points: Radio waves — TV, radio broadcasting, mobile communications; long wavelength passes around obstacles
Microwaves — satellite communications, cooking (absorbed by water molecules in food), radar
Infrared — thermal imaging cameras, remote controls, optical fibre communications, grills and heaters
Visible light — human vision, photography, lasers, optical fibres
Ultraviolet — sterilisation of water and surfaces, detecting forged banknotes (fluorescence), sunbeds, insect vision
X-rays — medical imaging of bones and teeth (absorbed by dense tissue), airport security scanners, checking welds
Gamma rays — treating cancer (radiotherapy — kills tumour cells), sterilising medical equipment, detecting tumours (PET scans)

sections.title: Hazards of EM Radiation
sections.text: Higher-frequency EM waves are ionising — they can damage living cells by removing electrons from atoms, potentially causing mutations and cancer.
points: Ionising radiation — UV, X-rays and gamma rays can ionise atoms, damaging DNA and causing cancer
Ultraviolet hazards — causes sunburn, premature skin ageing, eye damage (cataracts), skin cancer; more at higher frequencies
X-ray hazards — ionising; repeated exposure increases cancer risk; minimised by lead shielding and limiting dose
Gamma ray hazards — most ionising; controlled use in medicine; lead and thick concrete used for shielding
Non-ionising — radio waves, microwaves and infrared are non-ionising; microwaves heat tissue (mobile phone concerns unproven)
Dose matters — the risk depends on frequency, intensity and duration of exposure

keyTerms.def: Family of transverse waves ranging from radio waves to gamma rays, all travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum
3 × 10⁸ m/s — the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum (also written as c)
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, potentially causing cell mutations and cancer
EM waves just below visible light in frequency; emitted by warm objects; detected as heat
EM waves just above visible light in frequency; causes fluorescence; ionising at higher frequencies; causes sunburn
Highest-frequency EM waves; produced by nuclear decay; most ionising; used in cancer treatment
Lowest-frequency, longest-wavelength EM waves; non-ionising; used in communications and broadcasting
EM waves between radio and infrared; used in satellite communications and cooking

examTips: All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum — this is given in the AQA equation sheet but you must know when to apply it. Use v = fλ with v = 3 × 10⁸ for any EM wave calculation.
Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy per photon = more ionising — you can be asked for any one of these for any part of the spectrum. Learn the chain.

Learn the mnemonic for order: 'Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns'. AQA frequently asks you to place EM waves in order and identify which has greatest frequency, energy or shortest wavelength.

For hazards questions: state whether the radiation is ionising, what it can do to cells (damage DNA, cause mutations, cancer), and one safety precaution (lead shielding, limiting exposure time, sunscreen).
commonMistakes: Saying radio waves are the most energetic — gamma rays have the highest frequency and most energy; radio waves have the least.
Forgetting that all EM waves travel at the same speed in vacuum — students often say gamma rays travel faster because they have more energy. Speed is constant; energy depends on frequency.
Confusing wavelength order with frequency order — higher frequency = shorter wavelength. Radio waves have the LONGEST wavelength but LOWEST frequency.
Listing the EM spectrum in the wrong order — use the mnemonic and practise writing it out (Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, UV, X-ray, Gamma).
clozePassages: The electromagnetic spectrum is a family of transverse waves that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). In order of increasing frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and more energy. All electromagnetic waves can be reflected, refracted, and diffracted, and can travel through a vacuum.

Radio waves are used for communication — broadcasting, TV, and mobile phones. Microwaves are used for satellite communication and cooking. Infrared radiation is emitted by warm objects and used in remote controls and thermal imaging. Ultraviolet radiation from the sun causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer. X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, making them useful for medical imaging. Gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and treat cancer.

Different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum interact with matter in different ways. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage living cells, causing mutations and cancer. Ultraviolet radiation can cause skin cancer by damaging DNA. Infrared radiation is felt as heat. Microwaves can heat water molecules in food. Radio waves are non-ionising and pose no known health risk at normal exposure levels. The ozone layer protects Earth from most harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Black Body Radiation.intro: All objects absorb and emit radiation. The balance between these processes determines an object's temperature.
Black Body Radiation.mnemonic: "Hotter objects Emit More, Shift Shorter" — as temperature increases: more radiation emitted, peak shifts to Shorter wavelengths (Higher frequency). 'HEMSS' — Hotter → Emit More → Shift Shorter.

sections.title: Absorbing and Emitting Radiation
sections.text: Every object continuously absorbs and emits electromagnetic radiation. The temperature of an object depends on the balance between these two processes.
points: All objects emit infrared — every object above absolute zero emits EM radiation due to its temperature
Temperature equilibrium — temperature is constant when rate of absorption = rate of emission
Temperature rising — if absorbing more than emitting (e.g. object placed in sunlight), temperature rises
Temperature falling — if emitting more than absorbing (e.g. object in cold environment), temperature falls
Hotter objects — emit more radiation overall AND the peak of emission moves to shorter wavelengths (higher frequency)

sections.title: Black Body Radiation
sections.text: A black body is a theoretical perfect absorber and emitter. Real objects approximate this behaviour to varying degrees.
points: Perfect black body — absorbs ALL incident radiation (none reflected or transmitted); emits maximum radiation for its temperature
Black body spectrum — the emission spectrum has a characteristic shape; peak wavelength depends only on temperature
Stefan's law — total power emitted increases sharply with temperature (proportional to T⁴)
Peak wavelength shift — hotter object: peak shifts to shorter wavelength; red-hot → orange → white as temperature increases
The Sun — behaves approximately as a black body at ~5500°C; peak emission in visible light
Earth — behaves as a black body at ~15°C; peak emission in infrared (longer wavelength than the Sun)

sections.title: The Earth's Temperature and Greenhouse Effect
sections.text: Earth's temperature is determined by the balance between absorbed solar radiation and emitted infrared. Greenhouse gases disrupt this balance.
points: Energy balance — Earth's temperature stable when energy absorbed from Sun = energy emitted by Earth as infrared
Greenhouse gases — CO₂, methane, water vapour absorb infrared emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions
Greenhouse effect — gases reduce the rate of emission to space → Earth warms until a new, higher equilibrium temperature is reached
Enhanced greenhouse effect — increasing CO₂ from burning fossil fuels increases trapping of infrared → global warming
Albedo — reflective surfaces (ice, clouds) reflect sunlight, reducing absorption; melting ice reduces albedo, causing further warming

callout.label: Energy Balance
callout.text: Earth's temperature is stable when energy absorbed from the Sun = energy emitted by Earth. Greenhouse gases reduce emission → temperature rises to establish new balance.

keyTerms.def: A perfect absorber and emitter of radiation — absorbs all incident radiation and emits maximum radiation for its temperature
Electromagnetic waves emitted by all objects due to their temperature; felt as heat
The distribution of radiation emitted by an object across different wavelengths; shape depends only on temperature
The wavelength at which an object emits most strongly; decreases (shifts to shorter wavelength) as temperature increases
Gas (e.g. CO₂, CH₄) that absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface, reducing the rate of heat loss to space
Natural warming of Earth caused by greenhouse gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation
State where rate of absorption of radiation equals rate of emission, so temperature remains constant
The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface; snow and ice have high albedo

examTips: Temperature is stable when absorption rate = emission rate — AQA asks you to explain what happens if one side of this balance changes (e.g. more greenhouse gases). Always say the temperature rises until a new equilibrium is reached.

Hotter objects emit more radiation at shorter wavelengths — you may be given a graph of emission spectra at different temperatures. The peak moves left (to shorter wavelength) and the curve is higher as temperature increases.
Greenhouse effect: gases absorb Earth's infrared → reduce rate of emission to space → Earth warms. You must use the phrase 'rate of emission' not just 'traps heat' for full marks.

For 6-mark questions on climate change: mention energy balance, role of greenhouse gases absorbing infrared, re-emission in all directions, reduced rate of energy loss, rise in temperature, and enhanced effect from burning fossil fuels.
commonMistakes: Saying black objects always absorb radiation — this is about black bodies (theoretical perfect absorbers), not the colour black. A black body is a scientific concept, not a physical colour.
Forgetting that all objects emit infrared — not just hot ones. Even cold objects emit radiation; hotter objects just emit more and at higher frequencies.
Saying the greenhouse effect is bad — the natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. It is the ENHANCED greenhouse effect (from human activity) that causes concern.
Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone layer — the greenhouse effect relates to infrared retention; the ozone layer blocks UV. They are separate phenomena.
clozePassages: All objects emit electromagnetic radiation — the hotter the object, the more radiation it emits and the higher the frequency of the peak emission. A black body is an ideal absorber and emitter of radiation. It absorbs all radiation that falls on it and emits the maximum possible radiation at each wavelength for its temperature. The Sun behaves approximately like a black body at about 5500°C and emits most strongly in the visible part of the spectrum.

The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and also emits radiation. The balance between absorbed and emitted radiation determines Earth's temperature. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, warming the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations trap more radiation, causing the Earth's average temperature to rise — this is the enhanced greenhouse effect.

The intensity and wavelength distribution of radiation emitted by a body depends only on its temperature. As temperature increases, the peak of the emission shifts to shorter wavelengths (higher frequencies). This is why objects glow red, then orange, then white as they get hotter. The concept of black body radiation was crucial in developing quantum theory — classical physics could not explain the observed emission spectrum, leading Planck to propose that energy is emitted in discrete packets called quanta.
